newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEAR AND LOATHING STALK SEX SCANDAL RIDDEN BELGIUM.
newsitem.headline: FEAR AND LOATHING STALK SEX SCANDAL RIDDEN BELGIUM.

text.p: A mood verging on hysteria is sweeping Belgium, with a child sex and murder scandal prompting floods of denunciations in what some people have likened to the anti-communist paranoia of 1950s America.

To capture the atmosphere Le Soir newspaper ran a cartoon on Wednesday showing a man with binoculars peering through a shuttered window and saying into a telephone: "Yes judge, every morning he drives three children to school and hugs them."
"There is a sort of McCarthyism in the country against anyone with a past," Kris Deschouwer, Professor of Political Science at Brussels Free University, said.
"Of course things happened, there has been corruption and wrongdoing so that has to come into the open. But any little sin being the origin of being treated as a gangster is dangerous," he added.

"Things have gone too far...We have entered into a climate of incrimination where everyone denounces each other...It is starting to make me scared," prominent child rights activist Marie-France Botte said in an interview with Le Soir.
She said her organisation daily received hundreds of letters containing denunciations, as did similar groups. A special hot line set up by the gendarmerie has taken thousands of calls.
"I appeal for calm because I have the impression that people are using the paedophile problem to settle scores," Botte said.
The denunciations range from sex abuse to graft and corruption, and cover all walks of life from neighbours to politicians and the judiciary.

The allegation against Deputy Prime Minister Elio di Rupo of having had sex with under-age boys, a charge he angrily rejects, is the first direct denunciation of a government minister but by no means the first whiff of scandal against a public figure.
Alain Van der Biest, a former government minister, was arrested in September in connection with the 1991 murder of francophone Socialist Party patriarch Andre Cools.

One public prosecutor in Liege, known locally as the Palermo of the north because of its large Italian community and links to organised crime, is being investigated over allegations of paedophilia. Another is being probed over alleged graft.
A well-respected philanthropist has been accused of forcing himself on a young woman two decades ago.

On Friday the small, linguistically divided nation described variously as either Europe's cross-roads or its capital, will have suffered 100 days of torture since the rescue of two sexually abused girls from a house owned by Marc Dutroux.

The subsequent discovery of the bodies of four other murdered girls, revelations of police bungling, judicial dithering and suspicions of political interference have shattered public confidence and triggered calls for change.

Last month 250,000 people took to the streets of Brussels for a march that was intended to show support for the victims of sexual abuse and their parents but which rapidly turned into a demonstration of disgust with what is seen as a corrupt system.

Last week the parents of two of the murdered young girls called for the resignation of Interior Minister Johan Vande Lanotte, holding him responsible for bungling by the gendarmerie and threatening to call another mass rally if he refused.
The march, if it took place, could turn ugly given the mood in the country, observers said.
